journal: JOURNAL OF PARK AND RECREATION ADMINISTRATION
title: An Examination of the Guided Night Hiking Experience in Parks and Protected Areas
setting: recreation (guided night hikes on park and forest trails: a strenuous 3-mile hike at Table Rock State Park and an easy 'owl prowl' at Congaree National Park, South Carolina, and a moderately difficult 1.5-mile hike at Pisgah National Forest, North Carolina; ranger interviews also from Acadia National Park, Maine)
design: qualitative (phenomenological semi-structured interviews with night hikers and interpretive rangers; verbatim transcription, open and axial coding after Miles & Huberman 1994 and Strauss & Corbin 1998; triangulation and informant checks)
sample_n: 35 interviewees (31 night hikers - Table Rock 10, Congaree 11, Pisgah 10 - plus 4 interpretive rangers; hiker interviews averaged 17 min, range 9-39 min; ranger interviews averaged 33 min, range 17-53 min)
exposure: In-situ night-time acoustic environment of guided hikes, described by participants rather than measured or manipulated: nocturnal natural sounds (owls, cicadas, crickets, frogs, night bugs, a distant coyote or dog, wind in the trees, a babbling creek) and the 'natural quiet' produced by less human and traffic noise at night ([page 88]-[page 89], printed pp.79-80; [page 92]-[page 93], pp.83-84). No sound level measurement, acoustic index or experimental sound manipulation is reported. Reverse side: the recreational behaviour itself - choosing to hike at night rather than by day, hiking in guided groups of 10 to 30 people, whispering when communicating, and keeping artificial lights off - is reported to shape the acoustic environment and the salience of its perception ([page 90], p.81; [page 92]-[page 93], pp.83-84).
behaviour_measure: Self-reported recreation behaviour elicited by a common semi-structured interview script: (a) participation in guided night hiking rather than day hiking, the stated motivations for it and stated willingness to hike at night again ([page 88], p.79; [page 91], p.82); (b) in-group vocal behaviour during the hike - whispering and talking less to protect natural quiet ([page 90], p.81; [page 93], p.84); (c) keeping artificial lights off and stepping 10-15 feet away from the group at stops ([page 90], p.81; [page 94], p.85). No counts, frequencies or durations are reported - the authors state that the themes 'do not represent a frequency of comments' ([page 87], p.78).
measurement_method: self-report (semi-structured interviews with 31 hikers and 4 interpretive rangers, recorded and transcribed verbatim; the lead researcher joined the hikes to build rapport but no systematic observation data are reported)
key_finding: Night soundscapes, together with the night sky, were one of the two sensory attributes that defined the night hiking experience and were raised by respondents when asked about enjoyment, favourite aspects, motivations, outcomes and willingness to hike at night again, with owls, cicadas, crickets, frogs, a distant coyote and a creek named repeatedly ([page 88]-[page 89], pp.79-80). Conversely the night activity reshaped the acoustic experience: with limited visibility hikers relied more heavily on hearing, which drew attention to both night sounds and the lack of sound, and most participants said they deliberately whispered while communicating in order to protect natural quiet, while rangers added that too much artificial light may quiet nocturnal animals ([page 93], p.84; [page 94], p.85). Quietness at night, together with limited visibility, was also the reason respondents gave for an increased sense of both group and individual solitude despite hike group sizes of 10 to 30 ([page 90], p.81).
effect_stats: NR (qualitative study; the authors state explicitly that the themes 'do not represent a frequency of comments' ([page 87], p.78) and report no counts or statistics for the sound-behaviour relation)
